title: Patch & Exploit Watch: Ivanti VPN zero-day chain - why one patch was not enough
description:
Attackers chained three zero-days in Ivanti Connect Secure, the SSL VPN many companies use for remote access, to get root on the appliance without logging in. Here is how the chain worked, what the attackers went after, why devices patched on October 13 are still exposed, and what to do this week.

Timeline (2026)
- October 3: attacks begin against a fully patched appliance (Volexity).
- October 13: Ivanti discloses and fixes the first flaw, CVE-2026-104935.
- October 29: Ivanti patches two more, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527.
- October 30: the US agency CISA adds both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The chain (per Volexity)
1. Bypass the login check (CVE-2026-104935).
2. Run code through a file upload race (same CVE).
3. Escalate to root (CVE-2026-111357).
Afterwards the attackers took stored credentials and searched Active Directory for Windows LAPS admin passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. No web shell was left, logs were edited, and Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool did not detect the activity.

The catch
Versions fixed for the first flaw, such as 22.8R2.5, are still open to the two newer flaws. Fixed releases: 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 - check Ivanti's advisory for your branch.
CISA deadlines for US federal agencies: November 2 (CVE-2026-111357, plus forensic triage) and November 13 (CVE-2026-118527).

What to do this week
1. Upgrade every Connect Secure appliance to a fixed release.
2. Do not trust a clean Integrity Checker scan on its own.
3. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting.
4. If compromise is suspected, rotate the exposed credentials.
